title: Why Cats Can't Taste Sweetness
central_fact: Domestic cats carry an unexpressed Tas1r2 pseudogene, so the two-part sweet-taste receptor cannot form.
takeaway: A cat's indifference to sweets is receptor biology, not pickiness or a preference for expensive food.

hook.text: Your cat can't taste sugar. Here's why.

scenes.narration: Your cat can't taste sugar. Here's why.

visual.description: An orange tabby cat sits on a sunlit kitchen windowsill, looking directly into the lens with a calm, neutral expression. A small ceramic dish of sugar cubes sits far in the foreground, ignored. Soft morning light, realistic fur detail.
visual.subject: one orange tabby cat with clear tabby stripes and green eyes
visual.motion: slow push-in; the cat blinks once
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, cat's face in the upper middle third, dish blurred at the bottom edge
visual.continuity: same orange tabby, windowsill, and kitchen in every scene

scenes.narration: Cats are obligate carnivores. Meat is their main fare. Their sweet-taste equipment is missing a critical part.

visual.description: The same orange tabby eats from a shallow bowl of plain shredded meat on a clean kitchen floor. An owner's hand sets the bowl down and withdraws. The cat eats calmly; the sugar dish from the opening is visible but untouched on the counter above.
visual.subject: the same orange tabby and a human hand, no visible face
visual.motion: gentle tilt down from counter to bowl
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, cat and bowl in the lower middle third, clean negative space above
visual.continuity: same cat, kitchen, bowl, and sugar dish; no other animals

scenes.narration: In 2005, researchers examined the gene for Tas1r2, one of two proteins that build a working sweet receptor.

visual.description: A macro study of the same orange tabby's face as it laps water from a bowl. The tongue curls naturally, whiskers stay symmetrical, and the nose and eyes remain anatomically correct. Water ripples in slow motion.
visual.subject: the same orange tabby's tongue, nose, and whiskers
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, tongue and water in the lower third, one eye visible above
visual.continuity: same tabby markings and green eye; no collar or harness

scenes.narration: In cats, that gene has a 247-base-pair deletion and premature stop signals. It is a pseudogene, not expressed.

visual.description: A restrained abstract animation on a deep amber background: two translucent protein-like forms drift toward each other. One form is complete; the other has a clean gap and dissolves before they can join. No labels, equations, or readable characters appear.
visual.subject: two soft translucent molecular forms, one incomplete
visual.motion: slow orbital drift, then the incomplete form fades
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, the two forms centered with generous negative space
visual.continuity: same amber palette and grain as the kitchen scenes; no sudden style shift

scenes.narration: The partner gene, Tas1r3, is still expressed. But without both halves, the receptor cannot detect sugars. Sweetness has no channel to the brain.

visual.description: The same orange tabby sniffs a small dish of sugar cubes on the kitchen counter, then turns its head away and steps toward the meat bowl. The cat's movement is unhurried and curious, not disgusted.
visual.subject: the same orange tabby between a sugar dish and a meat bowl
visual.motion: single smooth lateral follow as the cat turns away
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, both dishes visible at the lower edges, cat centered
visual.continuity: same counter, dishes, and cat; sugar cubes remain uneaten

scenes.narration: The same broken gene appeared in six domestic cats, a tiger, and a cheetah. It is not pickiness. It is deep cat biology. No sweet tooth; just a carnivore's toolkit.

visual.description: A brief, respectful montage of three felines: the same orange tabby on its windowsill, a tiger standing in tall grass, and a cheetah on open savanna. Each shot is calm and observational, then the film returns to the tabby in warm window light.
visual.shot_type: three static wide portraits, then a close-up
visual.subject: orange tabby, tiger, and cheetah as separate realistic felines
visual.motion: slow cross-dissolves between the three portraits
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, each animal centered with natural habitat context
visual.continuity: natural coat patterns, correct feline anatomy, no fantasy hybrids

claims.text: Domestic cats are obligate carnivores and do not prefer sweet-tasting compounds.
claims.evidence_level: peer-reviewed comparative genomics and behavior review
claims.limits: Individual cats may still sample sweet foods; the claim concerns species-typical taste preference.

claims.text: The cat Tas1r2 gene has a 247-base-pair deletion and premature stop codons and is an unexpressed pseudogene.
claims.limits: The finding is based on studied cats and taste tissue; it does not quantify every possible residual sweet response.

claims.text: Tas1r3 is expressed in cat taste buds, but without functional Tas1r2 the sweet-receptor heteromer cannot form.
claims.limits: The receptor model is inferred from the two-part T1R2/T1R3 system established in other mammals.

claims.text: The same Tas1r2 deletion and stop codons were found in six domestic cats, one tiger, and one cheetah.
claims.limits: Small number of individuals per wild species; the claim is about the detected variants, not every member of each species.

claims.text: A cat's lack of interest in sweets is better explained by receptor biology than by pickiness.
claims.limits: Behavior is also influenced by learning, texture, smell, and familiarity; receptor loss is not the only factor.

visual_policy.style: Warm, tactile food-and-science documentary illustration with macro details and one restrained abstract sequence.
visual_policy.anatomy: One orange tabby with symmetrical tabby stripes, green eyes, a natural pink tongue, and correct whisker placement. The tiger and cheetah are separate, realistic felines with correct coat patterns.
visual_policy.welfare: The cat eats plain meat and is never shown eating sugar, chocolate, or unsafe human food. No restraint, fear, or forced interaction.
visual_policy.continuity: Same cat, kitchen, windowsill, ceramic dishes, and morning light. The abstract sequence keeps the same amber palette and grain.
visual_policy.disclosure: Illustrative, AI-assisted visuals; not documentary footage.

notes: Say the receptor cannot form, not that cats have no sense of taste at all.
Keep the abstract sequence non-literal; do not animate a textbook diagram with labels.

risk_notes: Do not imply cats should be fed sugar or that sweets are safe.
Do not claim every felid has been tested; the study sampled one tiger and one cheetah.
